name: WiFi Nugget (ESP8266)
one_line: ESP8266 (D1 Mini) board with OLED screen, 4 buttons and a neopixel, pre-flashed with a Wi-Fi deauther; open-source firmware also does SSDP phishing pages and deauth-attack detection.
why_notable: Open-source ESP8266 deauther hardware, originating from the community project at github.com/skickar/WiFiNugget (also used for the HakCat-Tech HaxxDetector deauth-detection firmware) and sold assembled by Retia — a cheap alternative deauth platform to the ones already tracked.

name: USB Nugget (ESP32S2)
one_line: ESP32-S2 board with native USB, OLED screen and buttons that enumerates as a USB flash drive and HID keyboard for drag-and-drop keystroke-injection (BadUSB) payloads, remotely controllable over Wi-Fi.
why_notable: Open-source BadUSB platform with its own 'Nugget OS' firmware and CircuitPython payload repos (RetiaLLC/RubberNugget-CircuitPython, RetiaLLC/S2-Nugget on GitHub) — functionally a Wi-Fi-controlled, mass-storage-loadable alternative to the USB Rubber Ducky already in the DB.

name: Bluetooth Nugget (ESP32S3)
one_line: ESP32-S3 board (dual-core successor to the USB Nugget) adding native BLE to the existing Wi-Fi monitor-mode and USB-HID keystroke-injection capability; screen and 6 buttons for on-device payload selection.
why_notable: Adds BLE attacks (demoed publicly sending pairing-request popup spam to nearby phones) to the open-source Nugget line, and is the base board for Retia's LoRa Meshtastic backpack add-on.

name: Solder Your Own Nugget Kit
one_line: Unassembled kit (PCB, SH1106 screen, 4 buttons, neopixel, 3D-printed case, plus a D1 Mini ESP8266 and an S2 Mini ESP32-S2 board) that the buyer solders into either a WiFi Nugget or a USB Nugget.
why_notable: Same open-source hardware/firmware as the WiFi Nugget and USB Nugget entries, just sold unassembled as a soldering-practice SKU — flagging as likely a duplicate device in different packaging rather than a distinct product.

name: LoRa Radio Backpack for USB & Bluetooth Nuggets (RFM95)
one_line: RFM95 LoRa radio add-on board (selectable 868MHz or 915MHz) that plugs onto a USB Nugget or Bluetooth Nugget for long-range wireless, exposing UART/SPI/I2C for extra peripherals.
why_notable: Vendor explicitly markets this as enabling 'long-range bad USB attacks' — it's sold specifically to extend the range/reach of the already-listed USB/Bluetooth Nugget BadUSB devices, plus adds Meshtastic support.

name: Open Source Meshtastic Nibble
one_line: Open-source RFM95 LoRa (868/915MHz) mesh-networking node built around an RP2040 or ESP32-S3, sold as bare PCB, unsoldered kit, or fully soldered; runs Meshtastic firmware for encrypted off-grid mesh comms.
why_notable: Fully open-source (github.com/retiallc/nibble), debuted at 38C3 alongside a 'Hacker's Guide to Meshtastic' talk; flagged borderline because its core function is encrypted mesh networking/comms rather than an offensive or defensive security-testing primitive, though it's squarely hacker-con hardware.

name: Nibble Screen Connect
one_line: ESP32-S3 board with a Semtech SX1262 LoRa radio, OLED screen, 2 buttons and a BME280 sensor, breadboard-compatible, for a hand-held Meshtastic or Meshcore mesh node.
why_notable: More expandable open-source Nibble variant (adds Meshcore support alongside Meshtastic); same borderline reasoning as the base Nibble — it's mesh comms hardware, not an attack tool.

name: Nibble Zero
one_line: ESP32-S3 + LoRa mesh node (Meshtastic, Meshcore, or Reticulum firmware) with a 3D-printed case and BMP280 sensor that can be flashed and operated directly from a Flipper Zero.
why_notable: Notable for direct Flipper Zero integration — the Flipper flashes and controls the node — bridging an already-cataloged device (Flipper Zero) into LoRa mesh networking; same comms-vs-attack-tool borderline reasoning as the other Nibble variants.

name: Newsheen Hacker Smart Cat Lamp Kit (pre-assembled)
one_line: ESP32-S3 board with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built into a squishy cat-shaped desk-lamp enclosure; reflashable into an audio-reactive light, internet radio, or a Meshtastic/Meshcore/Reticulum mesh node.
why_notable: 'Newsheen' appears to be the OEM/brand of the underlying smart-lamp reference hardware; Retia resells it with open hacker firmware access to its ESP32-S3 (Wi-Fi/BT, upgradable to a LoRa mesh node) — the same 'known board plus community firmware' relationship called out for other entries, just in a lamp enclosure instead of a display or dev board; borderline since it ships and is marketed primarily as a lamp.

name: NFC Placard Mystery Pack
one_line: Pack of 3 random passive NFC tags (mix of NTAG213/NTAG215, some glow-in-the-dark) mounted on placards styled to blend into urban signage; writable for URL redirection or Amiibo-style emulation.
why_notable: Passive tags with no onboard logic of their own — closer to a consumable than a device; flagged borderline low-confidence since the DB scope explicitly covers RFID/NFC but also excludes generic items with no capability of their own.
